plan: [I have value $24. With the common-component structure, a high own value signals others may also have high values (winner’s curse). In a second-price auction it’s sensible to shade my bid below my full value to avoid overpaying while still winning when I truly have the highest value. I pick a modest shading of $2 to trade off win probability and expected surplus.]

[Common-value component creates a winner's curse: winning tends to mean opponents had lower signals, so the second-highest bid conditional on winning is likely close to my signal. Therefore I will shade my bid below my private value (14). Because 14 is below the population mean, my chance to win is small; a conservative bid balances avoiding overpayment and capturing surplus if others are also low. I choose a modestly shaded bid of 10.0.]

[I have a private value of $28. In a second-price (Vickrey) auction, bidding your true value is the standard strategy: you win whenever the price (second-highest bid) is below your value and never overpay. There is a common-value component, but with no history to adjust beliefs, truthful bidding maximizes expected payoff and avoids leaving profitable wins on the table.]
